arml-2005-power-01a.title: Find the first difference
arml-2005-power-01a.body:
$h_1=110110110\ldots$ and $h_2=1001\ldots$. The first digits agree ($1$), the second digits differ ($1$ vs $0$), so $n=2$ and $d(h_1,h_2)=2^{-2}=\frac14$.

**Answer: $\frac14$**

arml-2005-power-01b.title: First difference in place 3
arml-2005-power-01b.body: $d(h_1,h)=\frac18=2^{-3}$ means $h$ agrees with $h_1=110110\ldots$ in the first two places and differs in the third place. The third digit of $h_1$ is $0$, so $h$ must begin $111$, and anything may follow. Three examples: $\overline1=111\ldots$, $1110\overline0$, and $111\overline{01}$.

arml-2005-power-01c.title: First difference in place 4 or later
arml-2005-power-01c.body:
$d(h_1,h)<\frac18=2^{-3}$ means the first difference occurs in place $4$ or later, so $h$ agrees with $h_1=110110110\ldots$ in the first three places. Take addresses that differ from $h_1$ first in place $4$, $5$, $6$; since $h_1$ has digits $1,1,0,1,1,0,\dots$,

- $h=1100\overline0$ (differs in place $4$, $d=\frac1{16}$),
- $h=11010\overline0$ (differs in place $5$, $d=\frac1{32}$),
- $h=110111\overline0$ (differs in place $6$, $d=\frac1{64}$).

**Answer: e.g. $1100\overline0$, $11010\overline0$, $110111\overline0$**

arml-2005-power-01d.title: Both directions
arml-2005-power-01d.body:
If $h=h'$, then $a_i=b_i$ for all $i$, so $D=\varnothing$ and $d(h,h')=0$ by definition.

If $h
e h'$, the addresses differ in at least one place, so $D
e\varnothing$ and has a smallest element $k$ (every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element). Then $d(h,h')=2^{-k}
e0$. Hence $d(h,h')=0$ only when $h=h'$. ∎

arml-2005-power-02a.title: Compute three distances
arml-2005-power-02a.body:
Post office $=000000\ldots$, school $=001001\ldots$, hospital $=00110011\ldots$.

- $d(\text{post office},\text{school})$: first difference in place $3$: $2^{-3}$.
- $d(\text{school},\text{hospital})$: $001001\ldots$ vs $001100\ldots$: first difference in place $4$: $2^{-4}$.
- $d(\text{post office},\text{hospital})$: first difference in place $3$: $2^{-3}$.

The trip via the school has length $\frac18+\frac1{16}=\frac3{16}$ and the direct trip has length $\frac18$, a difference of $\frac3{16}-\frac18=\frac1{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{16}$**

arml-2005-power-02b.title: Look at the first place where $h_1$ and $h_3$ differ
arml-2005-power-02b.body: Let $n$ be the first place where $h_1$ and $h_3$ differ, so $d(h_1,h_3)=2^{-n}$. Let $b$ be the $n$-th digit of $h_2$. Since the $n$-th digits of $h_1$ and $h_3$ differ, $b$ differs from at least one of them, say from the $n$-th digit of $h_i$ ($i=1$ or $3$). Then $h_2$ and $h_i$ differ in some place $m\le n$, so $d(h_2,h_i)\ge2^{-n}=d(h_1,h_3)$. Therefore one of the two terms on the left is already at least $d(h_1,h_3)$, and the sum is too. ∎

arml-2005-power-02c.title: Powers of two
arml-2005-power-02c.body:
Write $d(h_1,h_2)=2^{-a}$, $d(h_2,h_3)=2^{-b}$, $d(h_1,h_3)=2^{-c}$ with positive integers $a,b,c$ (the addresses are distinct). Suppose $2^{-2a}+2^{-2b}=2^{-2c}$; by symmetry assume $a\ge b$. Multiply by $2^{2a}$:
$$1+2^{2a-2b}=2^{2a-2c}.$$
If $a>b$ the left side is odd and greater than $1$, so it is not a power of $2$, a contradiction. If $a=b$ the left side is $2=2^1$, which would need $2a-2c=1$, impossible because $2a-2c$ is even. ∎

arml-2005-power-02c.title: Using the triangle inequality
arml-2005-power-02c.body: By Problem 2b, one of $d(h_1,h_2)$, $d(h_2,h_3)$ is at least $d(h_1,h_3)$. Then $d(h_1,h_2)^2+d(h_2,h_3)^2>d(h_1,h_3)^2$ (both squares are positive), so equality is impossible. ∎

arml-2005-power-03a.title: Choose addresses with a single $1$
arml-2005-power-03a.body: Let $h_n$ be the address with a $1$ in place $n$ and $0$ everywhere else. Then $h_n$ and $h_{n+1}$ first differ in place $n$ (digit $1$ versus $0$), so $d(h_n,h_{n+1})=2^{-n}$. The route is desirable and its length is $\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\cdots=1$.

arml-2005-power-03b.title: Strictly decreasing powers of two
arml-2005-power-03b.body: Each distance is positive (a strictly decreasing infinite sequence of distances that are $0$ or powers of $2$ cannot reach $0$ and keep decreasing), so $d(h_i,h_{i+1})=2^{-n_i}$ with integers $n_i\ge1$. Strict decrease means $n_1<n_2<n_3<\cdots$, so $n_i\ge i$. Hence the total length is at most $\sum_{i\ge1}2^{-i}=1$, which is finite. ∎

arml-2005-power-04a.title: Prepend any three digits
arml-2005-power-04a.body: Mail addressed to $abc\,h$ is delivered to $h$ (the first three digits are deleted). The Smiths' address is $\overline{1100}$, so they receive the mail addressed to $abc\overline{1100}$ for any digits $a,b,c$. One example is $100\overline{1100}=1001100\,1100\ldots$.

arml-2005-power-04b.title: Count the prefixes
arml-2005-power-04b.body:
Mail addressed to $h$ is delivered to $h$ with its first three digits removed. The Smiths receive the mail of exactly the addresses $abc\overline{1100}$, where $a,b,c$ are arbitrary digits. There are $2\cdot2\cdot2=8$ choices, giving $8$ different addresses (one of which, $\overline{1100}$ itself, is the Smiths' own address).

**Answer: 8**

arml-2005-power-05a.title: Find an address unchanged by deleting three digits
arml-2005-power-05a.body: A building receives its own mail when deleting the first three digits of its address gives back the same address, i.e. $a_{i+3}=a_i$ for all $i$. An address with period $3$ such as $\overline{101}=101101101\ldots$ works: deleting $101$ leaves $101101\ldots$ again.

arml-2005-power-05b.title: Addresses with period dividing 3
arml-2005-power-05b.body:
A building with address $a_1a_2a_3\ldots$ receives its own mail iff deleting the first three digits gives the same sequence: $a_{i+3}=a_i$ for all $i$. That holds exactly when the address is $\overline{abc}$ for some digits $a,b,c$ (each block of three is repeated). Each of $a,b,c$ can be $0$ or $1$, so there are $2^3=8$ such addresses (this includes the post office $\overline0$ and the address $\overline1$).

**Answer: 8**

arml-2005-power-06.title: Own mail means periodic
arml-2005-power-06.body:
Suppose the machine deletes the first $k\ge1$ digits. A building with address $a_1a_2a_3\ldots$ receives its own mail iff $a_{i+k}=a_i$ for all $i\ge1$, i.e. iff the address is $\overline{a_1a_2\cdots a_k}$ (a purely periodic address with a block of length $k$).

Therefore a building receives its own mail for some number $k$ of deleted digits exactly when its address is purely periodic, i.e. consists *solely* of a repeating block from the first digit on (equivalently, as a binary fraction it is a fraction in lowest terms with odd denominator). The buildings that never receive their own mail are exactly those whose address is **not** purely periodic: for example $1\overline{10}=1101010\ldots$ (its tail repeats, but not from the first digit) or $11010010001\ldots$ (the runs of $0$s grow).

arml-2005-power-07a.title: Insertion is one-to-one
arml-2005-power-07a.body: Mail addressed to $h$ goes to $1001h$. If $1001h_1=1001h_2$, then removing the common first four digits gives $h_1=h_2$. So two different addresses are never sent to the same building: **No**.

arml-2005-power-07b.title: Take the periodic address
arml-2005-power-07b.body: Let $M$ be the inserted string. The building with address $\overline M=MMM\ldots$ has mail sent to $M\,\overline M=MMM\ldots=\overline M$, which is the same address. So it receives its own mail. ∎

arml-2005-power-08a.title: Agree on the first four places
arml-2005-power-08a.body: $d(h,h_i)<\frac1{16}=2^{-4}$ means the first difference is in place $5$ or later (or there is none), i.e. $h_i$ agrees with $h=1100\ldots$ in the first four places. So $N\!\left(h,\frac1{16}\right)$ consists of all addresses $1100h'$ where $h'$ is any address. Examples: $1100\overline0$, $11001\overline0$, $110011\overline0$.

arml-2005-power-08b.title: Look at first digits
arml-2005-power-08b.body:
Addresses at distance more than $\frac1{16}$ from the post office $\overline0$ are those that first differ from $\overline0$ in place $1$, $2$ or $3$: distance $\frac12$ (address starts with $1$), $\frac14$ (starts $01$), $\frac18$ (starts $001$). So the set contains addresses starting with $1$ and others starting with $0$.

Suppose this set were $N(x,r)$ with $r<\frac12$. Every $h$ in it satisfies $d(h,x)<\frac12$, so $h$ cannot differ from $x$ in the first place (that would give distance $\frac12$). Hence all addresses in $N(x,r)$ have the same first digit as $x$. But the set contains addresses beginning with $0$ and addresses beginning with $1$, a contradiction. **No.** ∎

arml-2005-power-09.title: Radius half the distance
arml-2005-power-09.body:
Suppose $h_1,h_2$ first differ in place $n$, so $d(h_1,h_2)=2^{-n}$. Let $r_1=r_2=2^{-(n+1)}$. If an address $x$ lay in both neighborhoods, then
$$d(h_1,h_2)\le d(h_1,x)+d(x,h_2)<2^{-(n+1)}+2^{-(n+1)}=2^{-n}=d(h_1,h_2),$$
a contradiction. So the two neighborhoods are disjoint. ∎

arml-2005-power-10.title: Binary and ternary expansions of numbers in $(0,1]$
arml-2005-power-10.body:
Let $B$ be the set of all infinite $0$-$1$ sequences (old addresses) and $T$ the set of all infinite $0$-$1$-$2$ sequences (new addresses). Let $E_B\subset B$ be the sequences that end in an infinite string of $0$s, and $E_T\subset T$ likewise.

**Main part.** Every real number $x\in(0,1]$ has exactly one binary expansion $x=\sum a_i2^{-i}$ that does not end in all $0$s (using the expansion ending in all $1$s for dyadic numbers, e.g. $\frac12=0.0111\ldots_2$), and exactly one ternary expansion $x=\sum c_i3^{-i}$ that does not end in all $0$s. So the map $B\setminus E_B\to(0,1]$ taking a sequence to its binary value is a bijection, and so is $T\setminus E_T\to(0,1]$. Composing the first with the inverse of the second gives a bijection $\varphi:B\setminus E_B\to T\setminus E_T$: send $a_1a_2\ldots$ to the ternary digits of the number whose binary digits it is. (For example $\overline{10}=\frac23$ maps to $\frac23=0.2222\ldots_3$, i.e. to $\overline2$.)

**The leftover sequences.** $E_B$ is countably infinite: the sequences with all digits after place $n$ equal to $0$ form a finite set ($2^n$ sequences) for each $n$, and $E_B$ is the union over $n$; it is infinite. Likewise $E_T$ is countably infinite. Hence there is a bijection $\psi:E_B\to E_T$ (list the elements of each set as $e_1,e_2,\ldots$ and send $e_i\mapsto f_i$).

Putting $\varphi$ and $\psi$ together gives a bijection $B\to T$: every old address receives exactly one new address, and every new address is used exactly once. ∎
